results, or conclusions; neglect means overlooking relevant material supplied in

This variant uses PyAgent's text-action protocol rather than API function calls.
Return exactly one single-line action per response:
Action: tool_name(<JSON object>)
Start directly with Action:, without prose or Markdown fences. Do not repeat the
action or add a second action: only the first action will execute. Wait for its
observation before choosing the next action.
For example:
Action: read_pages({"start": 2, "end": 3, "reason": "Inspect the experimental setup."})
All tool arguments must satisfy the supplied contracts, including reason. Put
only a brief observable purpose in reason; do not output a Thought section or
private chain-of-thought. JSON strings must escape embedded newlines and quotes.
Finish only by calling submit_review with the complete review object. Do not
emit FINISH or other completion markers. Tool errors are observations: correct
the next action. An accepted submission ends the run without another model call.

pages.text: There is a trade-off in ID/OOD performance when choosing between full ﬁnetuning and lightweight ﬁnetuning: full ﬁnetuning consistently outperform in-distribution, whereas lightweight ﬁnetuning consistently outperform out-of-distribution (Li & Liang, 2021; Lester et al., 2021). To quantify this trade-off, we examine the generation performance of both methods on ID and OOD data. As shown in Table 2, when evaluating in-distribution, full ﬁnetuning achieves the stronger results (denoting this ID skyline as 100%), whereas lightweight ﬁnetuning achieves only 81% of the skyline, on average. When evaluating out-of-distribution, lightweight ﬁnetuning achieves stronger result (denoting this OOD skyline as 100%), whereas full ﬁnetuning achieves only 84% of the skyline. Lightweight ﬁnetuning tends to produce models that are more robust at the cost of good ID performance; Full ﬁnetuning produces models that attain good ID performance at the cost of OOD performance. 3

pages.text: As we observe in Section 5, full ﬁnetuning models attain better ID performance but worse OOD performance, whereas lightweight ﬁnetuning models attain better OOD performance at the cost of good ID performance. Is it possible to achieve both good ID and OOD performance simultaneously? In this section, we show that a simple ensemble of the two methods accomplishes this. First, we train a lightweight ﬁnetuning model p ( (cid:96) ) and a full ﬁnetuning model p ( f) on D train . At decoding time, we combine the prediction of the p ( (cid:96) ) and p ( f) by interpolating them at each token. At each time step t , both models output a next token distribution conditioned on the common history y <t , and the two distributions are interpolated with a mixture weight λ . The output is generated by beam searching the ensemble distribution p (Ens) ( y t | x, y <t ) . 3 Though it is worth noting again that for open-domain QA, we performed a small amount of manual, exploratory hyperparameter optimization to optimize the ID of full ﬁnetuning and the OOD of lightweight ﬁnetuning. 5 three , and ensembles with mixture coefﬁcients in each chosen by in-distribution validation performance. The ± reports standard deviation, estimated across 5 seeds.
6.1 C HOOSING THE M IXTURE W EIGHT λ

We start with a set of { λ i } K i =1 where λ i ∈ [0 , 1] . For example we use λ ∈ { 0 ., 0 . 1 , 0 . 25 , 0 . 5 , 0 . 75 , 0 . 9 , 1 . 0 } in this experiment. We choose the mixture weight λ i that attains the best score on D val . This method of choosing λ is useful because (1) it crucially does not use OOD data, which is typically unaccessible at model selection time, and (2) it guarantees that ID performance is not sacriﬁced, because we can match ID performance by setting λ = 0 .
